 MEMPHIS, Tenn. — Thousands fewer Tennessee households are receiving federal food assistance compared with a year ago, putting additional pressure on the Mid-South Food Bank as families struggle to afford groceries ahead of the holiday season.
 According to state data cited by FOX13, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) enrollment declined from approximately 152,000 in September 2025 to 136,000 in September 2026, a decrease of 16,000.
 The decline represents a drop of approximately 10.5% over the one-year period.
 SNAP provides monthly benefits to eligible low-income households to help purchase groceries.
 But as enrollment declines, the Mid-South Food Bank says more families are turning to local food assistance programs to help make ends meet.
 According to the Mid-South Food Bank, getting approved for SNAP benefits has become increasingly difficult.
 Food bank officials say changes to program rules have contributed to more applicants being denied assistance.
 During the first six months of 2026, the organization helped 404 people submit SNAP applications.
 Of those applicants, only 65 were approved, according to the food bank.
 That represents an approval rate of approximately 16%.
 The organization did not provide a breakdown of why the remaining applicants were denied or whether some applications were still pending.
 Nicole Willis, a spokeswoman for the Mid-South Food Bank, said the challenges are creating additional demand for emergency food assistance.
 "When people aren't getting their SNAP benefits, lines get longer, people are hungrier," Willis said.
 "And so we see it, especially with our partner agencies. And when they need more food, you know, they reach out to us to get more."
 The Mid-South Food Bank works with partner agencies to provide food assistance to residents across the region.
 Willis said the organization is seeing the effects of families struggling to access SNAP benefits, particularly through increased demand at its partner agencies.
 When households lose access to food assistance or are unable to qualify for benefits, some turn to food pantries and community organizations to help cover their grocery needs.
 That creates additional pressure on food banks responsible for supplying those organizations.
 The decline in Tennessee's reported SNAP enrollment comes as many families continue facing financial challenges associated with everyday expenses.
 However, the state enrollment figures alone do not establish why individual households stopped receiving benefits.
 With Thanksgiving approaching, the Mid-South Food Bank is encouraging residents to help families experiencing food insecurity.
 Willis said community members do not have to make financial contributions to support the organization's work.
 Donating food from a household pantry can also help families who are struggling to put meals on the table.
 The organization says donations are particularly important as its partner agencies seek additional supplies to meet demand.
 For Willis, the need extends beyond the holiday season as families continue navigating challenges with food assistance.
 The Mid-South Food Bank is urging residents who are able to help to consider donating food or supporting local hunger relief efforts.
